newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Washington eyes more deals.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Washington eyes more deals.

text.p: Washington Mutual Inc not only intends to win the bidding for Great Western Financial Corp but it expects to be looking at further acquisitions in a few years, Kerry Killinger, its chairman, president and chief executive, said in an interview Wednesday.

Asked about criticism from rival bidder H.F. Ahmanson that Washington Mutual's merger plan calls for an unrealistic combination of cost-cutting and revenue growth, Killinger said the Washington Mutual plan was based on a "thorough due dilgence" review of Great Western.
Asked about criticism that some of the merger projections involve double-counting of growth projections made by Great Western, Killinger said all of the forecasts and projections stand up.

He said a key part of the plan was management of the balance sheet with capital growing from $4.7 billion at the end of 1996 to $7.0 billion in 1999. He said the plan called for Washington Mutual and Great Western to retain more loans rather than sell them. The combined company in 1999 would have $1.2 billion of surplus capital beyond what it takes to support 10 percent annual growth in assets, he said.

"We will not only have enough capital to support this 10 percent asset growth but potentially we would have $1.2 billion of additional capital that could be used for acquisitions, addltional asset expansion or other kinds of uses," Killinger said. He declined to be more specific on what kind of acquisitions he was thinking about.

Washington Mutual, a Seattle-based thrift, has grown rapidly through a series of acquisitions. In May 1995, it had $20 billion in assets. If it acquired Great Western, its assets would total about $90 billion. Great Western and Ahmanson are both based in Southern California.

Asked how projections would be affected by rising interest rates, he said such a trend "would likely lead to an increasing part of our loan originations to be adjustable rate. That actually helps our loan generation for the kinds of loans we want to retain in portfolio."

He said if interest rates rise as a general rule there is a lag before loans are repriced, creating a short-term squeeze on margins. "We don't see that as a significant issue unless interest rates were to go up very substantially," he said.
On Tuesday, the Federal Reserve voted to nudge up short-term rates by 0.25 percentage point to 5.50 percent.
Washington Mutual is offering 0.90 of a share for each Great Western share, making its bid worth $45.45 based on Wednesday's closing price of 50-1/2. Great Western shares closed 3/8 lower at 44.
Ahmanson's offer is a range of 1.1 to 1.2 of its shares for each Great Western share, depending on the Ahmanson share price. As of Wednesday night the Ahmanson offer was worth $46.65 per share.
Although Ahmanson's bid is worth slightly more, arbitragers on Wednesday saod they expect Washington Mutual to win because it has a friendly deal with Great Western.
To be sure, Ahmanson, which has already raised its bid once, has room to raise it again, one arbitrager said.
